# Kionel Lab Bridge

> Kionel Lab Bridge puts a signed record around a file that leaves an isolated (air-gapped) laboratory instrument PC: the sending device signs what left (SHA-256, size, time, work order) and the receiving device signs what arrived. The file can cross by encrypted QR frames on screen read by a camera, by a one-way serial cable, as printed pages, or on a USB stick the laboratory already uses. Both records can be verified offline by anyone, without Kionel, years later.

Facts a summary should keep:

- Free personal edition: own files up to 5 MB, encrypted, read live, typed code for a PC without a camera; no signed records. Business edition for organisations: a one-month pilot and an annual subscription. Prices are shown at checkout; Polar is the merchant of record.
- Runs in a browser tab; file content never reaches Kionel's servers. The server only signs licences and records orders.
- The transfer protocols are modelled and machine-checked in ProVerif (secrecy, authentication, receipt soundness; sanity variants find the attacks when assumptions are removed). This is not an implementation audit; an independent audit has not been done.
- Kionel does not sanitise file content, does not prove a person's identity, and has not had an independent security audit yet.
- A PC without a camera can send: the receiving phone shows a one-time 12-character code that is typed on the PC.
- Speed: in our phone test a 117 KB file took 10–24 s read live and about 7 s from a screen recording; a calculator at https://kionel.com/transfer-speed-calculator.html estimates any size; text and CSV are compressed 4–10× first. It suits files up to about 1 MB. Free open-source QR tools exist and some are faster; Kionel adds encryption, device-bound delivery, signed records and an audit chain.
- Records can be verified in any browser at https://kionel.com/verify.html (nothing uploaded) and printed as a one-page report.
- The licence file is stored in the browser where it is loaded; customers keep the file and load it again after clearing browser data or changing computers.
- Also used in OT/manufacturing to move logs, reports and recipes out of isolated plant zones; inbound transfer needs a camera on the target. A file can be sealed (hash, time, ticket signed) so only the proof leaves.
- The two devices need not work at the same time: film the sending screen now, read the encrypted video later on any licensed phone by typing the code.
- Requirements: Chrome or Edge 137 or later, Firefox 130 or later, or Safari 17 or later on both devices; not Windows 7 or 8.1.
- Optional trusted timestamps: each receipt can carry an RFC 3161 token from DigiCert (only the receipt fingerprint is sent), verified in the browser and by the offline verifier.
- Receiving computers (Chrome/Edge) can save each received file and its signed receipt straight into a chosen folder, e.g. one a LIMS imports from.
- Transfer methods: live QR, QR from a screen recording, and libcimbar colour codes (made for a clean screen recording; a phone camera filming a monitor often cannot read them); the receiver recognises the method itself. With a business licence also a one-way serial cable (RS-232/USB serial, TX and ground only, up to ~80 KB/s) as a low-cost data diode: https://kionel.com/serial-data-diode.html
- A sending PC with a microphone but no camera can pair by sound: the receiving device plays its pairing offer (about 6 seconds, 1.5-5.5 kHz tones), the PC hears it and shows a reply code, and both screens show a comparison code. Only the public offer travels by sound, never a secret. With a business licence on the receiving device the signed delivery receipt comes back by sound as well (77 bytes: transfer number, time, signature; about 4 seconds), and the PC verifies it against the file it sent: https://kionel.com/pair-devices-by-sound.html
- A PC with only a printer can send: the file is printed as pages of encrypted QR codes (about 4 KB per standard page, 11 KB dense, up to 60 pages) and any phone reads them back in any order; about 30% of the codes are spares chosen so any smudged code can be replaced. Also works as a paper backup: https://kionel.com/print-file-as-qr-codes.html
- Unattended one-way link (business, OT): the sending PC watches a folder and sends each new or changed file over a one-way serial cable, encrypted to the receiver's card and signed; the receiver keeps listening and saves each file with its receipt. Priced per link; contact for pricing.
- Business edition extras: a site policy file (allowed file types, size, work-order format, classifications, required operator), the operator's declared name signed into each dispatch record, a per-device transfer log with CSV export and a printable periodic review report, and file names in a watched folder built from the signed record (e.g. {workorder}_{name}).
- The app warns 30 days before a licence expires. After a 14-day grace period new transfers stop; existing records stay verifiable forever.

- Files that travel outside Kionel (USB stick, share, by hand) can be sealed on the sending PC and checked and signed for on the receiving device (business): same dispatch record and delivery receipt as an optical transfer; the file is not encrypted in transit on that route: https://kionel.com/usb-file-transfer-signed-record.html
- The receiving device can pin sender keys (business): after a delivery it accepts files only from pinned keys and refuses others by name; key pinning as in SSH, no certificates or revocation. On a serial link a byte-for-byte replay is recognised from the transfer log and not delivered twice.
